item.title: Sweet cherries ride wave of China's booming market demands

Cherries are seen at a cherry orchard in Curico province, central Chile, Nov. 14, 2026. Chile is a major global exporter of cherries, and China is the largest overseas market for Chilean cherries. According to data from Chile's Ministry of Agriculture, about 569,000 tonnes of cherries were exported in the 2025/2026 season, of which about 87 percent went to China. In recent years, against the backdrop of deepening economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region, China and Chile, both the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies, have continued to advance economic and trade cooperation. Since 2018, Chile has operated a direct shipping route to China known as the "cherry express," significantly shortening the transit time. This year marks the APEC "China Year," and the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting was held in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19. Taking this as an opportunity, China and Chile will further strengthen cooperation on trade facilitation and agricultural trade. The cherries crossing the Pacific Ocean have become a vivid epitome of the deepening economic and trade cooperation between China and Chile. item.title: As Chinese universities use AI detectors to screen theses, questions arise over accuracy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
BEIJING, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- After five rounds of revisions, one student still had a thesis flagged as 30 percent AI-generated by an artificial intelligence (AI) detector. Such results have become a source of anxiety for many graduating students in China. As AI detection tools become more widely used in thesis reviews, some universities have made the "AI rate" a formal requirement alongside conventional plagiarism checks. A paper that passes the plagiarism check can still be barred from thesis defense if its AI rate exceeds the permitted threshold. But the reliability of this technology is increasingly in question. Some detection platforms have flagged passages from classic Chinese literary works, including Zhu Ziqing's "Moonlight over the Lotus Pond" and writings by Lu Xun, as more than 80 percent AI-generated. These cases highlight a problem facing universities as they try to regulate generative AI: a single percentage says little about how much intellectual work a student has actually done. Four scholars in the fields of law, communication and education, speaking to Xinhua, said the AI rate should not serve as a decisive standard. WHY DETECTORS ARE INCONSISTENT Commercial AI detectors use AI to identify AI-generated writing, said Zhang Linghan, head of the institute of AI law at China University of Political Science and Law. They analyze statistical features such as perplexity and burstiness, assuming that machine-generated prose is unusually fluent and standardized while human writing varies in rhythm. Given the probabilistic method, no tool is fully accurate, she said, and a percentage alone "cannot serve as reliable evidence of academic misconduct." Wang Feng, dean of the School of Communication at East China Normal University, said AI detection differs fundamentally from plagiarism screening. Plagiarism checks compare papers against existing texts and identify sources of overlap. AI detectors, by contrast, rely on algorithmic rules rather than traceable source texts. Results can vary across platforms using different data and algorithms, and can even differ when the same paper is submitted to the same platform at different times, he said. Classic works can be flagged because the stylistic conventions detectors treat as markers of AI writing largely derive from classic literature, Wang added. Xiong Bingqi, head of the 21st Century Education Research Institute in Shenzhen, south China, noted that plagiarism checks, introduced in China more than 20 years ago, had never resolved questions of originality: students could evade them by rewording or rearranging borrowed text. AI detectors, he said, similarly cannot determine whether a paper is original or innovative. WHERE THE LINE IS The limits of detection matter because students may use AI to search academic literature, polish language, draft an outline or generate an entire paper -- activities with very different academic implications that current detection tools cannot distinguish. Zhang said the key question is whether the student's own contribution remains "substantive and dominant." Using AI for literature searches, language polishing or formatting generally should not be treated as misconduct and may need no or only brief disclosure, she said. AI-generated outlines are also generally acceptable, provided students check them for factual errors. But if AI contributes to a paper's core ideas or directly generates text used in its main body, such use must be disclosed, she said. Wang, whose university was among the first in China to issue guidelines on students' use of AI, said East China Normal University initially set a 20-percent limit on directly generated content. The limit applied only to text used without subsequent changes, while text students revised and adapted to their research should not count as directly generated. He also cautioned against judging papers based on their so-called AI feel: scientific writing is often formulaic, and academic value should rest on originality, not prose style. Chu Zhaohui, a research fellow at the China National Academy of Educational Sciences, stressed that AI cannot replace original research based on real circumstances, experiments and data. He cited two instances in which AI had fabricated material: a sentence generated by AI and circulated online under his name, and a student assignment citing a nonexistent article attributed to him, complete with a title, journal name and page numbers. Despite these limitations, many Chinese universities have adopted percentage limits on the "AI rate" because they are relatively easy to administer and can serve as a deterrent, Zhang said. But she warned that the thresholds lack strong scientific support, risk penalizing legitimate AI use and have fueled a gray market in services promising to lower AI-detection scores. Rigid scoring rules can also push students into meaningless rewriting just to lower their AI scores, Zhang said. A better approach, she argued, would allow AI use with transparent disclosure, strengthen process-based evaluation and adviser oversight, and gradually reduce reliance on a single quantitative measure. WHAT A THESIS SHOULD MEASURE The debate over AI detection ultimately raises a more fundamental question: what should a university thesis demonstrate? For Chu, the central issue is not AI but evaluation itself. A good paper should address questions others have not explored or offer insights that advance existing understanding, he said. Theses built on repetition, piles of references or superficial formalities had little value even before AI, and the technology has only made their weaknesses more apparent. Universities, he said, should give greater weight to process-based evaluation while also assessing the final work for its research substance and by the standards of the academic community. Zhang called for combining institutional rules with human judgment. Universities should assess students throughout the research process, from topic selection and research proposals to fieldwork, writing and the final defense, she said. Substantive judgments about a paper's originality, rigor and research value should be left to advisers and peer experts, with an appeals process for disputed decisions. Xiong said closer supervision could also reduce reliance on detection tools. Advisers who follow students from topic selection through research and writing can identify many problems before a thesis is completed. Wang emphasized the role of teachers in making this shift work. Rather than simply barring students from using AI, universities should invest more in improving teachers' AI literacy and exploring how the technology can be integrated into teaching and research. Teachers, he said, should help students explore appropriate uses of AI, guide them in its application and provide academic oversight. The four scholars' views converge on one conclusion: academic integrity cannot be reduced to a numerical score. A thesis should be judged not by whether a student stays below an AI rate threshold, but by whether the student can pose meaningful questions, investigate them via genuine research and arrive at independent conclusions. ■

item.title: China's tech innovation engine powers a connected Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
* China's push to unleash the potential of innovation and share technological dividends through open regional integration has resonated widely -- translating its innovation capacity into broader market opportunities and lending fresh momentum to economic growth and the building of an Asia-Pacific community. * Across the Asia-Pacific, China's technological innovations are finding applications in a growing range of industries and aspects of everyday life. * The release of the Shenzhen Initiative marked a milestone in the 30-year history of the APEC CEO Summit. It was a historic moment in Shenzhen, a city that has stood at the forefront of China's opening-up and has grown into a global innovation hub. BEIJING, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- As host of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China has placed openness, innovation and cooperation at the heart of its agenda as the three priority areas. Throughout this week's sessions, participants explored how the Asia-Pacific can navigate structural shifts and cultivate new engines of economic growth. China's push to unleash the potential of innovation and share technological dividends through open regional integration has resonated widely -- translating its innovation capacity into broader market opportunities and lending fresh momentum to economic growth and the building of an Asia-Pacific community. INNOVATION THAT BENEFITS ALL At an experimental durian orchard at Chiang Mai University in Thailand, agricultural lecturer Supakorn Wongsuk prepares a drone for takeoff. Having studied in China, he now applies the technology to explore more efficient methods of cultivating tropical fruits. Lifting smoothly into the air, the drone glides above rows of durian trees, releasing a fine mist of pesticide across their leaves and branches. "Using drones to spray pesticides can improve operational efficiency, reduce farmers' direct exposure to chemicals, and protect their health and safety," said Supakorn. He sees the Chinese innovations as offering benefits that extend well beyond farming efficiency. "For young people, drone operations can also create new job opportunities." Across the Asia-Pacific, China's technological innovations are finding applications in a growing range of industries and aspects of everyday life. The role of innovation also drew sharp focus at the APEC CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen. "Innovation is very important, and innovation cannot be done overnight. It requires strong education support and accumulated experience. This is where we think China can play a role," said Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry Chairman Anindya N. Bakrie. "China has an important role to play," said Julien Leclair-Dionne, associate director at the University of Ottawa's Professional Development Institute. "Particularly given its technological capabilities, innovation ecosystem and experience in scaling emerging technologies." "Ultimately, what matters most is not simply how advanced the technologies become, but how effectively the innovations are translated into opportunities for people, organizations and communities across the region," he said. OPENNESS CREATES OPPORTUNITIES Released on Wednesday, the Shenzhen Initiative of the APEC CEO Summit 2026 highlighted the transformative potential of frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence, while recognizing the accompanying risks and regulatory challenges that require coordinated regional oversight. At the heart of the document lies a clear, unified conviction among business leaders: no single economy can capture the promise of breakthrough technology -- or tame its disruptions -- alone; only deep regional cooperation can turn innovation into shared prosperity. Auckland Business Chamber CEO Simon Bridges emphasized the need for cooperation amid global uncertainty. "I think cooperation is probably the byword of APEC. And we know in the world right now, it's more important than ever," he said. China's approach to AI development provides "a very good example" that allows others to learn from its technological advances, he added. The appeal of Chinese AI models has become increasingly evident across the region. In South Korea, nearly half of the AI models released by local developers on Hugging Face, a globally popular open-source platform, between January and August this year were based on Chinese foundation models. "China has adopted AI with more open-weight, open-source, low-cost models that are going to be used by businesses around the world," said Jacob Cooke, CEO of WPIC Marketing + Technologies, a leading e-commerce and technology consultancy. "These Chinese companies have done their best to get this technology out to help people," Cooke said at the summit. The release of the Shenzhen Initiative marked a milestone in the 30-year history of the APEC CEO Summit. It was a historic moment in Shenzhen, a city that has stood at the forefront of China's opening-up and has grown into a global innovation hub. For Lee Ju-kwan, director of the National Center for APEC Studies at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy of South Korea, Shenzhen's relentless innovation engine came vividly into focus during a visit to electric vehicle giant BYD's headquarters, offering a firsthand look at the homegrown tech muscle powering the city. "I was deeply impressed by what I saw, particularly robots performing tasks that would traditionally be carried out by human workers on the production line," Lee said. "This year, by hosting APEC, China has taken the opportunity to put forward and renew initiatives aimed at promoting openness and cooperation. I believe these efforts deserve attention and support," Lee said. GREEN INNOVATION "It's the most fantastic ride," said Jeffrey Sachs, a professor at Columbia University, looking back on an epic 15,000-km summer odyssey from Rome to China's Hong Kong, retracing Marco Polo's historic path behind the wheel of a BYD electric vehicle. Sachs said the journey showed how far green technology had advanced. "The technology is already here. Most of it is in its most advanced stage in China," Sachs said during a high-level panel at the APEC CEO Summit 2026. He also noted that China had significantly reduced the cost of green technologies, making the transition more affordable. "To go green is not to make an extra burden for the sake of the planet. It's just to have a low-cost, resilient, state-of-the-art energy system," he said. The benefits of China's green innovation are also being felt by residents of Goulburn in New South Wales, Australia. With an integrated solar-and-storage solution supplied by a Chinese company, the local community has brought its own solar farm into operation. The facility began supplying electricity to the grid in March, with part of its annual profits to be channeled into a community fund to help residents facing energy poverty. "For a long time, it has been talk around the kitchen table. Suddenly here we are in amongst the panels, watching the sun send electrons to the people and my kids all own little parts of this with the community," said Goulburn resident Dave Suttle. "Without China's involvement, we definitely wouldn't have solar cells as cheap as now," Martin Green, Scientia Professor of Photovoltaic and Renewable Energy Engineering at the University of New South Wales, told Xinhua. Having worked with China's photovoltaic industry for more than four decades, Green is now collaborating with Chinese partners on the next generation of solar technology. "Working with China, we feel we're in a position to improve the solar performance more quickly," he said. ■

item.title: China's second homegrown large cruise ship begins maiden commercial voyage
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
A tourist interacts with a robot on Adora Flora City, China's second domestically built large cruise ship, on Nov. 22, 2026. Adora Flora City embarked on its maiden voyage on Sunday, marking a new step in the country's efforts to expand cruise tourism and boost consumption.(Xinhua) GUANGZHOU, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's second domestically built large cruise ship, Adora Flora City, embarked on its maiden voyage on Sunday, marking a new step in the country's efforts to expand cruise tourism and boost consumption. Carrying more than 3,800 passengers, the ship departed from Guangzhou in south China's Guangdong Province on a six-day, five-night journey to Hong Kong and Hue, Vietnam. Measuring 341 meters in length and with a gross tonnage of 141,900, the vessel has 2,130 cabins and can accommodate up to 5,232 passengers. Construction of Adora Flora City began in August 2022. Operated by Adora Cruises under China Tourism Group, the ship was delivered in Shanghai, east China, on Nov. 6 and embarked on its first trial voyage on Nov. 9. Shi Dai, chairperson of China Tourism Group, said the company is using cruise operations to drive the development of integrated cultural tourism products and travel experiences, aiming to set a new benchmark for vacations at sea. Adora Flora City is larger and features a more streamlined design than its sister ship, Adora Magic City, China's first domestically built large cruise ship. Adora Magic City began commercial operations in January 2024 and has since completed about 250 voyages. Hu Zhenyu, deputy director of the Qianhai branch of the China Development Institute, said the entry into service of two domestically built large cruise ships marks a new phase for China's cruise industry. The development will not only expand the range of high-quality marine tourism products but also create new drivers of consumption in coastal areas, Hu said. In 2027, Adora Flora City is scheduled to undertake over 50 international voyages from its home port in Guangzhou, offering both short getaways and longer itineraries to destinations including Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei. The ship will also offer voyages with no scheduled port calls, allowing passengers to enjoy the cruise ship as a destination in itself. The vessel departed from the Guangzhou Nansha International Cruise Home Port, one of China's largest integrated cruise port complexes. A duty-free store at the terminal also opened on Sunday, adding a fresh shopping option for cruise passengers. Wu Qingsong, deputy director of Guangzhou's culture, radio, television and tourism bureau, said the maiden voyage presents an opportunity for the city to better integrate its cruise port, shipping industry and tourism resources. Guo Jia, assistant vice president of product and guest experience at Adora Cruises, said the company plans to expand year-round operations across multiple home ports in east and north China, and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, offering passengers more high-quality cruise experiences. The maiden voyage comes as China seeks to expand tourism consumption. A 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for cultural and tourism development calls for boosting spending on cruise and yacht tours, among other specialized tourism offerings. China has seen strong growth in cruise tourism, with total cruise passenger throughput rising 25.3 percent year on year in 2025, according to the Ministry of Natural Resources. ■ This photo taken on Nov. 22, 2026 shows Adora Flora City, China's second domestically built large cruise ship, docked at the Guangzhou Nansha International Cruise Home Port in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province. item.title: China urges U.S. to revoke proposed telecom restrictions: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
BEIJING, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- China on Sunday called on the United States to revoke proposed restrictions on Chinese telecom operators' direct access to U.S. phone numbers, saying the move violates the principles of non-discrimination and fair competition. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) abused its regulatory powers and overstretched the concept of national security, while making arbitrary accusations against Chinese telecom companies without factual basis and maliciously undermining their operations in the United States, a commerce ministry spokesperson noted in response to a media query. The FCC has recently continued to push to decouple and sever supply chains between China and the United States in telecommunications, communications, testing and certification, the spokesperson added. Such moves run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and undermine the stability of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, the spokesperson said. China urges the United States to immediately rescind the measures and return to the right way of resolving issues through consultations, the spokesperson said, noting that China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests. ■

item.title: Forum on overseas studies of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era held in Uzbekistan
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
Participants attend a thematic forum of the 2026 edition of the International Forum on Overseas Studies of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era in Tashkent, capital of Uzbekistan, Nov. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Zafar Khalilov) TASHKENT, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- A thematic forum of the 2026 edition of the International Forum on Overseas Studies of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era was held Saturday in Tashkent, capital of Uzbekistan. Co-organized by the Institute of Russian, Eastern European and Central Asian Studies of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and the University of World Economy and Diplomacy of Uzbekistan, the forum was themed "China-Central Asia: High-Quality Belt and Road Cooperation and Green, Innovation-Driven Development." Participants noted that the "Book House for Xi Jinping's Works," which was inaugurated in January this year, serves as an important platform for China and Uzbekistan to deepen research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and exchange experience in state governance. They added that China's innovative proposal of the Belt and Road Initiative helps strengthen policy and strategic coordination among countries. The participants also said the forum's theme has strong practical significance. They stressed that when proposing new infrastructure and technical solutions for Central Asia, all parties should take full consideration of regional characteristics, the actual needs of each country and future development priorities, in which universities, research institutions and think tank experts play an important role. At the seminar, think tank experts and university scholars from China and Central Asian countries conducted in-depth discussions on topics including the Green Silk Road and the pursuit of sustainable development. ■

item.title: Xi Story: Bringing Hainan's rainforest back to life
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
HAIKOU, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- Zhou Zhaoli, a member of the Hainan gibbon monitoring team, starts his day at 4:30 a.m., long before sunrise. With flashlights in hand, he and his teammates pick their way through dense undergrowth in the mountainous Bawangling area of south China's Hainan Province, braving thorns and leech bites. Their reward is sometimes the sight of Hainan gibbons high in the forest canopy, and the sound of their distinctive calls echoing through the trees at first light. The world's 20 gibbon species live in 11 Asian countries, and most are in decline. Native to the island province's tropical rainforests, the Hainan gibbon was once pushed to the brink of extinction by commercial logging, deforestation and poaching. Today it is the only gibbon species in the world whose population has kept growing. During an inspection tour of Hainan in April 2022, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited part of these rainforests and asked local villagers whether they had seen the rare primates. At that time, the habitat hosted 36 gibbons in five groups. By the end of 2025, the figure reached 44 gibbons in seven groups, up from fewer than 10 in two groups in the early 1980s. Hainan's tropical rainforest is China's largest, best-preserved and most concentrated stretch of contiguous island-type tropical rainforest. The rainforest was once fragmented across more than 20 nature reserves and other protected areas in nine cities and counties. In 2019, Hainan began piloting an integrated approach, placing previously separate nature reserves, forest parks and state-owned forest farms under unified management. About two years later, the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park was established as one of China's first five national parks, which together span ecosystems from giant panda habitats in Sichuan, Gansu and Shaanxi provinces to the only home of the Hainan gibbon. Xi has closely followed the park's development. In 2018, he called for establishing national parks, including those protecting tropical rainforests. In 2019, he chaired a key reform meeting that approved a pilot plan for the Hainan national park. In 2021, he announced the establishment of China's first five national parks at the COP15 leaders' summit. During that 2022 inspection tour, Xi walked along a boardwalk in the national park, taking a close look at its natural environment. "He slowed his pace, studying the trees and listening closely to the sounds of nature as we walked," said Zheng Yan, a member of the park's public education and outreach team, who accompanied Xi and introduced the park to him during the visit. The park has improved markedly in both infrastructure and management capacity since its establishment, said Zheng, who has worked there for more than a decade. Xi's interest in rainforest conservation extends beyond China. On a visit to Brazil in July 2014, he recalled his 2009 trip to Manaus, a city deep in the Amazon rainforest, saying that protecting this vast expanse of pristine forest was vital to the global ecosystem. Protecting tropical rainforests is closely tied to humanity's survival and well-being, and it is a shared responsibility that calls for concerted global efforts. In recent years, China and Brazil have deepened cooperation on climate change and sustainable development. With support from the international community, the two countries are exploring new approaches to rainforest conservation and development, including measures that help local farmers improve their livelihoods and reduce deforestation while safeguarding the world's precious ecological assets and advancing global climate goals. Greice Quele Aparecida Barboza de Oliveira, an environmental analyst with Brazil's Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation, visited Hainan recently to learn about China's approach to biodiversity conservation and to see how the national park protects the rare primate. "These are areas I knew little about before. I am studying them closely so that I can take China's experience in wildlife conservation home with me," she said. She was in Hainan for the 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference, which ended on Sunday and drew international officials, experts and representatives from more than 20 countries. Climate change is becoming an increasingly serious challenge in Brazil and around the world, she said, adding that international cooperation and exchanges like those at the Hainan conference can help share effective conservation practices with other countries. During his 2022 visit to Hainan, Xi also asked about forest rangers' income and village-level public spending. He stressed the need to strictly protect tropical rainforests while ensuring that ecological conservation, green development and improvements in people's livelihoods go hand in hand. Hainan's tropical rainforest lies in one of the world's 34 biodiversity hotspots and serves as a reservoir of water, a source of food and wealth and a carbon sink. "Hainan's tropical rainforest does not belong to Hainan alone. It belongs to the people of the whole country and to Mother Earth as a whole. It is a national treasure," Xi said. ■

item.title: Xinhua Headlines: Why China-Russia-U.S. summit hailed historic for world stability, peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21
BEIJING, Nov. 21 (Xinhua) -- World leaders and observers spoke highly of the first-ever face-to-face meeting between the heads of state of China, Russia and the United States, saying the talks have brought the world hope for peace, stability and cooperation. Chinese President Xi Jinping chaired the historic summit in the city of Shenzhen, south China, on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump. As major countries and permanent members of the UN Security Council, China, Russia and the United States should set good examples, work together to meet global challenges, jointly uphold world peace and stability, and make greater contributions to the progress of humanity, Xi said. Following the summit, the three countries released the China-Russia-U.S. Heads of State Declaration toward Peace, outlining their common understandings on issues including the UN reform, energy security, the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court and nuclear risk reduction. LANDMARK STEP FOR GLOBAL SECURITY At a White House news conference on Friday, Trump hailed the Shenzhen meeting as "one of the most momentous international summits in many years." He said the "historic summit" had produced a trilateral peace declaration in which China, Russia and the United States reaffirmed that a nuclear war must never be fought. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said China's efforts to host the summit will help create and open up space for meaningful dialogue and mutual understanding toward lasting peace and harmony. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said the three leaders had shown wisdom and statesmanship in taking a step that mattered to the wider international community. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said he noticed how often the leaders had spoken of peace during their meeting. At the United Nations, Farhan Haq, deputy spokesman for the secretary-general, said the organization welcomed efforts by world leaders, including those of the Security Council's permanent members, to seek common solutions to global problems. Denis Simon, former executive vice chancellor of Duke Kunshan University, said the summit could open a new channel for dialogue on international security among the three countries whose decisions carry considerable military, economic and diplomatic weight. "I see the meeting as an important opening," said Paul Frimpong, executive director of the Africa-China Center for Policy and Advisory. With several international crises unfolding at once, he said, sitting together gave each leader a chance to hear directly from the other two about the risks they considered most pressing and where they saw room to act together. Gergely Salat, a senior researcher at the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, said the meeting showed that China has been maintaining channels with both Washington and Moscow and has enough credibility with both to bring them to the same table. "Few capitals could do that today," he said. FINDING RIGHT WAY TO GET ALONG At the summit, Xi made four points on how major countries could find the right way to get along and jointly underpin world peace, calling for mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, and dialogue and consultation. "China, Russia and the United States should continue to encourage parties to a conflict to sit down and talk, and settle disputes through political and diplomatic means," he said. Sourabh Gupta, a resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies in Washington, noted the repeated references at the summit to preserving the outcomes of World War II. As permanent members of the UN Security Council, the three countries bear a special responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, he said. Wang Yiwei, a professor at Renmin University of China's School of International Studies, said advances in artificial intelligence were adding a new layer of risk for nuclear powers. Against that backdrop, he said, China's emphasis on preserving strategic stability at the summit sent an encouraging signal about the prospects for peace. Shraga Biran, head of Israel's Institute for Structural Reforms, pointed to the Middle East, noting that with several regional flashpoints in play, reliable communication can keep one miscalculation from triggering another and reduce the risk that a crisis escalates by accident. ENCOURAGING CONSENSUS Xi called on the three countries to follow through on the consensus reached at the summit, strengthen communication, build common ground through dialogue, promote peace via cooperation, and work together to build a better world. Ezzat Saad, director of the Cairo-based Egyptian Council for Foreign Affairs, said that a better understanding among the major countries could give diplomats more room to work and help contain tensions across the Middle East region. "When fuel and freight costs rise, businesses pay more to move goods, and families can feel it in food prices," said Frimpong with the Africa-China Center for Policy and Advisory. In the heads of state declaration released following the summit, the three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows. In regions recovering from conflict, Frimpong said, more reliable energy supplies would also make it easier for businesses to reopen and invest. For Alphonse Muleefu, principal of the College of Arts and Social Sciences at the University of Rwanda, the declaration issued in Shenzhen showed that the three countries could find common ground. Building on it, he said, would take mutual respect, sustained dialogue and practical cooperation. "I believe this meeting marks an encouraging step toward a more stable world," he said.■
